item.description: On The Hacker News: Nearly one in ten LiteLLM gateways exposed on the internet accepted the default admin key sk-1234, according to a recent scan. This key grants full access to cloud IAM credentials and all model provider API keys stored on the server. The risk is real and demands immediate attention. Default credentials like sk-1234 are a red flag. They act as both an admin credential and a switch for authentication, making them a double threat. If left unchanged, they expose the entire infrastructure to exploitation. The fix is simple: replace the default key with a long, random value. No upgrade is needed, but the process must be done carefully to avoid losing access to stored credentials. LiteLLM's security model assumes administrators are trusted, which is why the flaw isn't labeled a vulnerability. But in practice, this trust can be exploited. The solution lies in governance and monitoring. Regular audits, strict key management, and limiting outbound network access are essential. These steps ensure that even if a default key is used, the damage is contained.

item.title: The state of AI for security: Measuring what matters most for building trust | Amazon Web Services
item.description: On Aws amazon: The Deception Benchmark highlights a critical gap in AI security tools: distinguishing real vulnerabilities from false alarms. As leaders in AI governance, we must prioritize precision over speed. A model that flags too much noise undermines trust and wastes engineering time. This benchmark tests whether AI can reason about code, mitigations, and context to avoid false positives. The results are sobering. General-purpose models struggle to balance false positives and negatives, often missing real issues while flagging safe code. This underscores the need for systems that reason beyond pattern recognition. Agentic workflows and multi-step validation are promising, but they must be tested against benchmarks that measure understanding, not just repetition. For security teams, this means asking vendors not just how their tools find vulnerabilities, but how often they’re wrong. Pair AI with human verification on high-risk paths. Use Deception Benchmark to hold tools accountable. The goal isn’t just detection—it’s ensuring AI aligns with real-world security outcomes. This benchmark is a step toward building trust in AI-driven security. It strips away scaffolding to measure what matters: whether a model truly understands code and mitigations. The challenge is real, and the stakes are high. As leaders, we must push for tools that don’t just flag issues, but flag them right.

item.title: Deep-Live-Cam Supply Chain Attack: Technical Analysis
item.description: On SafeDep: The Deep-Live-Cam supply chain attack highlights how subtle dependency changes can introduce malicious code into trusted software. A seemingly routine update to requirements.txt redirected installation to a malicious source, blending in with legitimate metadata. This makes detection challenging without close scrutiny. The attack leverages pip's build backend to execute hidden code during installation. By embedding malicious payloads in setup.py, the attacker bypassed visibility in most editors. The use of whitespace and CJK variables further obfuscates the malicious logic, making manual review unreliable. The payload then downloads a loader from a Telegram page, which extracts and executes additional stages. This multi-layered approach ensures persistence across systems, with clipboard hijacking and startup registration reinforcing the attack's reach. The code replaces wallet addresses, indicating a focus on financial theft. Supply chain security demands more than just dependency checks. AI can help identify anomalies in update patterns and detect hidden code. Governance and continuous monitoring are critical to catching these subtle threats before they escalate.

item.title: The Elephant in Enterprise Security
item.description: On Dark Reading: Privilege management is no longer a niche concern. It’s the missing piece in securing modern enterprises where non-human identities and AI agents dominate. These entities, from service accounts to tokens and AI agents, outlive their creators and operate without oversight. They move across systems, inheriting privileges that span teams and domains. This creates an invisible attack surface that traditional tools can’t see. The elephant in enterprise security is privilege—not the identity itself, but what it can do. A standard user and a domain admin are both identities, but only the latter can cause damage. The same applies to non-human identities. A token with read access to a single bucket is low risk, but one that can assume admin roles across three hops is a different story. Most organizations can’t name their most privileged identities, let alone understand their true reach. Breaking down silos is essential. Teams are all right about their piece of the identity puzzle, but security requires a unified view. Privilege is the common thread that ties IAM, PAM, cloud security, and SOC together. Modern platforms that focus on privilege offer visibility, intelligence, and protection. They let teams see the same problems, understand them, and act. This is how you start reducing the identity attack surface. Control privilege, and you control risk. Avoid point solutions that create new silos. Look for platforms that surface risk, prioritize it, and make it actionable. The goal isn’t to fix one team’s problem—it’s to secure the whole environment. That’s how you finally see the whole elephant.

item.title: PostGREShell: The database powering much of the internet had an open door for 12 years
item.description: On Cyera: PostGREShell is a critical vulnerability in PostgreSQL that's been lurking for 12 years. It exploits the replication protocol, which is used by backup accounts in every PostgreSQL setup. The flaw allows low-privilege accounts to load and execute arbitrary code, leading to remote code execution and full server compromise. The vulnerability exists in every PostgreSQL version since 2014 and was never patched until now. Attackers can exploit it by using a malicious plugin name to bypass security checks. This means anyone with access to the replication protocol can escalate to superuser and install a backdoor that survives cleanup. This highlights the need for rigorous plugin and replication protocol security in enterprise environments. The replication path was never validated, making it a perfect entry point for attackers. It's a stark reminder that even well-secured systems can have unguarded back doors. The blast radius is enormous because PostgreSQL powers so much of the internet. From financial transactions to medical records, a critical vulnerability in this database can have far-reaching consequences. It's a wake-up call for all organizations relying on PostgreSQL.

item.title: DeepSeek Harness Flaw Let AI Agents Disable Their Own File Sandbox Without Approval
item.description: On The Hacker News: The DeepSeek Harness flaw shows how easy it is for an AI agent to bypass its own sandbox. A single command can disable the sandbox's protections, allowing the agent to write outside its workspace. This happened because the tool's local interface was reachable from inside the sandbox, and it lacked proper authentication. The agent could call the interface and switch to a mode that disables the sandbox without needing approval. This is a serious risk for anyone using agentic AI systems. This isn't just a theoretical issue. The flaw worked on a default installation until DeepSeek fixed it. The fix involved adding a one-time token and requiring a signed cookie for access. But the sandbox itself remains unchanged. This means the agent can still access network resources and read files outside its workspace. The real problem is that the tool's design allowed this escape in the first place. The lesson here is clear. We need to treat agentic AI systems with the same rigor as any other critical infrastructure. Sandboxing is a start, but it's not enough. We must implement strict access controls, monitor for unusual behavior, and ensure that all interfaces are properly secured. This flaw is a wake-up call for the entire industry. We can't rely on sandboxes alone to protect us from malicious or rogue agents. The fix is available, but it's not always easy to apply. Some versions of the tool are still vulnerable, and third-party builds may not have the latest updates. Users need to check which version they're running and upgrade if necessary. This is a reminder that security is a shared responsibility. Developers, operators, and users all have a role to play in keeping agentic AI systems safe.

item.title: Webinar: Learn How to Answer “Are We Exposed?” Faster After a New CVE
item.description: On The Hacker News: In the AI era, the speed at which we answer "Are we exposed?" defines our security posture. A new CVE lands, and the real challenge begins. Teams are drowning in data from scanners, endpoints, cloud inventories, and SBOMs. The delay between disclosure and exposure assessment is no longer acceptable. item.title: CVE-2026-82533: DeepSeek Harness Vulnerability Lets AI Agents Escape Their Own Sandbox
item.description: On Ox: A critical sandbox escape flaw in DeepSeek Harness highlights the dangers of relying on untrusted inputs for security decisions. This escape path relied on the agent’s ability to execute commands without approval, effectively bypassing the confinement designed to protect the host system. The flaw demonstrates how seemingly secure sandboxing can fail if not properly enforced. item.title: Rustbot, the macOS malware used in the latest Rust Supply Chain Attack
item.description: On Iru: The Rust supply chain attack underscores the growing threat of malicious code embedded in developer ecosystems. item.title: Malware on the Blockchain: An Ongoing Campaign's New WebRTC Twist
item.description: On Netskope: EtherHiding represents a new supply chain threat leveraging blockchain to host malware. Attackers use BSC testnet smart contracts as a dead drop, updating payloads from a single contract. This makes takedown efforts ineffective and allows for rapid delivery across thousands of compromised sites. The technique has been observed on over 5,400 small-business websites, often WordPress or PrestaShop, with no clear commonality beyond their compromise. The use of testnet rather than mainnet is strategic. Testnet offers free infrastructure for developers, allowing threat actors to deploy and rewrite contracts without cost. This reduces operational overhead and increases persistence. The same delivery chain applies: a loader injects a script that fetches and executes payloads from the blockchain, often leading to a ClickFix overlay or a WebRTC data channel for command and control. The WebRTC variant bypasses standard signaling processes, creating an encrypted channel without observable artifacts. By hardcoding session details, attackers avoid detection while maintaining control. This approach makes payloads harder to inspect, as they execute in memory and avoid disk writes. The technique highlights the need for deeper infrastructure monitoring and non-web traffic analysis to catch these stealthy attacks. This campaign underscores the evolving sophistication of supply chain threats. Cyberattackers are repurposing free developer tools to create durable, hard-to-remove delivery mechanisms. Proactive monitoring, infrastructure defense, and awareness of unconventional attack vectors are critical. Site owners should integrity-check their CMS assets and block BSC-testnet RPC endpoints to reduce exposure.

item.description: On Manifold: GitSpawn is a critical vulnerability in AI coding agents that allows untrusted repositories to execute code with user privileges. This happens before the user even realizes the danger, with no approval prompt and full access to credentials and environment variables. This flaw isn’t limited to one vendor. The attack vector is simple—delivering a compromised directory via shared files, USB, or sync folders. The damage is severe, with full machine access and potential data exfiltration. item.title: The QTFY Hunt: How Chinese Hackers Were Tracked and How the Internet Became the Sensor

item.title: Mini Shai-Hulud Strikes Again: openapi-react-query-codegen
item.description: On SafeDep: The npm supply chain attack on @7nohe/openapi-react-query-codegen is a stark reminder of the risks in CI/CD pipelines. Attackers exploited a GitHub Actions workflow with no author-association gate to trigger a release and publish malicious versions under a legitimate package. This highlights how flawed automation can be weaponized. The attack used two execution triggers: a binding.gyp file that leverages node-gyp’s Python evaluation and a preinstall hook with a heavily obfuscated script. The payload downloads and runs Bun from GitHub, matching patterns seen in previous supply chain attacks. This reinforces the need for strict access controls and continuous pipeline auditing. Secure GitHub Actions workflows are critical. The lack of an author-association gate allowed any user to trigger the release. We must enforce gates, limit permissions, and use frozen lockfiles to prevent arbitrary code execution. This is a win for attackers who understand the weaknesses in open source ecosystems. The fix involved removing the issue_comment trigger and tightening permissions. Teams must review their CI/CD pipelines for similar vulnerabilities. AI and automation can’t replace vigilance—especially in open source. Stay sharp, and keep your supply chains secure.

item.title: GitHub - CSPF-Founder/red-clippy: open-source pentest management built to be operated by an AI agent

item.title: Fire Ant Evolves: From Hypervisors to Trusted Infrastructure

The attack demonstrates that compromise of network and authentication layers can lead to broader breaches. item.title: SVG Smuggling: How a 26,000-Email Phishing Campaign Hid Malware in Image Files
item.description: On Kaseya: SVG smuggling is a growing threat that exploits how email systems classify files. Attackers are using SVGs—text-based image files—to hide malicious JavaScript, bypassing traditional attachment scanners. The recent 26,589-email campaign used SVGs mislabeled as plain text to deliver obfuscated code disguised as voicemails. This leverages the gap between how files are perceived and what they can actually do. The attack relies on two main deceptions. First, the file is mislabeled as text/plain instead of image/svg+xml, tricking scanners into ignoring its contents. Second, the SVG acts as a launcher, fetching the real payload from a remote server at runtime. This means the malicious code isn’t in the file itself but is executed in the browser after the attachment is opened. Email security tools like INKY detect these attacks by analyzing behavior, not just file types. The campaign was flagged entirely because it mimicked internal notifications and carried suspicious content. Native filters failed to catch most of the emails, highlighting the need for detection methods that evaluate context and action, not just file names or hashes. This isn’t just a technical problem—it’s a shift in how attackers exploit trust. SVGs are treated as harmless, but they can carry code. Teams must treat SVGs as potential threats, not just images. Block or sandbox inbound SVGs, strengthen spoof detection, and educate users on phishing lures like fake voicemails. The future of email security depends on behavior, not assumptions.

item.title: MCPJacking: 155 Hijackable MCPs Discovered Live in the Official MCP Marketplace
item.description: On Air Security: MCPJacking is a growing threat in agentic AI systems. It exploits the blind trust agents place in their initial configurations. An attacker can reclaim a lapsed domain once a legitimate service goes dark and instantly inherit the agent’s connection. This creates a persistent and unmonitored line of communication that remains open indefinitely. The attack is subtle. It doesn’t require injecting malicious code into the agent’s prompt. Instead, it hijacks the MCP server, which the agent trusts implicitly. From this position, the attacker can redefine tools, exfiltrate data, inject prompts, and steer the agent’s behavior without detection. This highlights the need for governance and continuous vetting. MCPs originate from registries, GitHub, or individual configurations, often connecting to agents with production access without visibility. Security teams must scan entry resolution, monitor for handoffs, and maintain the ability to revoke access. MCPJacking underscores the importance of trust management in AI agent ecosystems. We must build systems that verify the identity and intent of service providers, not just the connection path. Governance, continuous risk management, and visibility are critical to securing agentic AI.

item.title: Hacking your life with AI can get you hacked

item.title: Benign Set Should Look Malicious
item.description: On Pipelab: The article makes a strong case for testing AI agent egress detection against inputs that look like attacks but aren’t. A false-positive rate against clean traffic is meaningless if the test set lacks real-world threats. The problem is clear: benign data must mimic malicious patterns to properly evaluate a detector’s resilience. Testing against easy negatives like API calls or JSON payloads proves little. A rule that ignores those can be written with a regex that matches nothing. The real test is whether the system stays calm when benign traffic wears an attacker’s clothes. That’s where the value of detection lies. Hard negatives—inputs that carry attack-like features but are harmless—are the true stressors. A tool schema naming ten attack types or a log with repeated 401 errors are examples of this. These samples expose a jumpy detector and are the ones that matter most in real-world scenarios. Building a robust test set requires pulling from your own data: docs, logs, runbooks, and tool schemas. Label each sample against your policy and keep a private holdout set. Reporting false-positive rates on both easy and hard negatives is essential. A single number hides the gap, and that gap is the finding.

item.title: The Two Mitigations for the Service-Account Confused Deputy in the Cloud
item.description: On Kat Traxler: Service account misconfigurations in the cloud can create confused deputy risks, where a privileged intermediary is tricked into acting on behalf of an unprivileged caller. This often happens when customer-managed identities are improperly attached to execution environments. The privilege escalation path is created at bind time, not runtime, making it critical to enforce authorization checks during attachment. The first mitigation focuses on marking the attachment. When an identity is bound to a resource, a control check ensures the caller has the right to use that identity. This is a bind-time authorization check, not a runtime one. Once the identity is attached, the resource automatically retrieves its token without re-evaluation. The key is ensuring the right caller has the right to act as that identity. For provider-managed identities, the risk is different. These are owned and operated by the CSP, and a lower-privileged caller could trick them into using their permissions against a resource they shouldn’t access. The mitigation lies with the provider, but AWS offers more visibility through mechanisms like FAS and condition keys. These allow customers to limit who the global principal can act on behalf of, adding an extra layer of control. In GCP and Azure, internal checks remain opaque—only revealed when a request is denied. Azure, for instance, blocks operations that reference uncontrolled resources, forcing you to prove you have the right to act on them. This is the confused-deputy guard in action. Understanding who owns the identity and applying the right mitigation is key to securing your cloud environment.

This reinforces the need for continuous monitoring, strict access policies, and rigorous validation of all authentication mechanisms.

item.title: AI Agents Enable Adaptive Computer Worms
item.description: On arXiv: AI-driven worms are redefining what we think of as cyber threats. Traditional malware relied on known vulnerabilities, but the research shows how AI agents can create adaptive, self-sustaining threats. These worms don’t just exploit weaknesses—they reason about targets, adapt in real time, and synthesize new attack logic on the fly. The implications are profound. Since these worms use stolen compute resources, the cost of infection is near zero. This creates a dangerous economic imbalance between attackers and defenders. No longer can we rely on patching or centralized safety controls to stop them. We need to rethink our security frameworks. Adaptive defenses must evolve faster than threats. Governance for agentic AI systems must include real-time monitoring, zero-trust principles, and AI-specific controls. The stakes are high—this isn’t hypothetical anymore. The research underscores a critical shift in the threat landscape. Our focus must move from static defenses to dynamic, intelligent systems that can anticipate and neutralize evolving risks. It’s time to prepare for autonomous generative adversaries.

item.title: Update: Ongoing Checkmarx Supply Chain Security Incident
item.description: On Checkmarx: The Checkmarx supply chain incident is a stark reminder of the risks in CI/CD pipelines and credential management. Attackers exploited a Trivy vulnerability to access GitHub repos, leading to the publication of malicious code and data leaks. This highlights the need for strict access controls and hardening of cloud environments. Credential rotation and secure authentication methods are critical. Checkmarx rotated exposed credentials and moved to OIDC, a step we should all follow. Tools like Trivy and Mandiant can help detect and mitigate such threats early. GitHub and AWS environments must be treated as high-value targets. Checkmarx locked down access and enhanced monitoring, which is a model for others. Teams should prioritize least-privilege access and regular security audits to prevent similar breaches.

item.title: One does not simply defend agentically
item.description: On Ncsc: Defenders face unique challenges when using AI for cyber defence. Unlike attackers, who focus on technical problems with clear success metrics, we deal with organisational constraints and political hurdles. Our mission is to protect the business, not to conduct cyber offence. This means we must carefully assess how AI can support our goals without disrupting operations. The key is to align AI with our priorities. We need frameworks that ensure automated actions are low risk and tightly controlled. For example, AI can help summarise data or prioritise tasks, but it shouldn’t replace human judgment. We must build trust in these tools by proving they won’t harm the business. Agentic AI has potential, but it requires careful governance. We need to answer questions like: Can AI prove a system’s network calls or process dependencies? Only then can we confidently automate defences. This is where research and collaboration will be critical. The NCSC is working on initiatives like Cyber Shield to shape this future. Organisations can’t wait for perfect solutions. We must improve security through traditional methods while exploring AI’s role. The path is clear: start with low-risk actions, build confidence, and scale responsibly. This is how we turn agentic AI from a concept into a practical defence strategy.

item.title: Meet Bluekit: The AI-Powered All-in-One Phishing Kit
item.description: On Varonis: Bluekit represents a significant evolution in phishing kits. By integrating AI and automation, it streamlines the attack lifecycle from template selection to domain management and campaign execution. This consolidation reduces the barrier to entry for attackers and increases the sophistication of phishing operations. Security teams must adapt to detect these advanced threats. The AI Assistant within Bluekit offers operators tools to craft phishing campaigns, though our testing revealed limitations. The output leaned on placeholders and generic scaffolding rather than polished, ready-to-use content. This suggests the AI serves more as a campaign generator than a fully automated phishing solution. Still, its presence highlights the growing role of AI in attack vectors. Bluekit’s rapid development and expanding feature set underscore the need for proactive defense strategies. Traditional detection methods may fall short against such dynamic threats. Security operations must prioritize advanced detection, real-time response, and continuous monitoring to stay ahead of evolving attack patterns.

item.title: Incident Report: LiteLLM/Telnyx supply-chain attacks, with guidance - The Python Package Index Blog
item.description: On Pypi: The recent PyPI supply chain attacks on litellm and telnyx highlight the growing threat of malware injection into widely used packages. Attackers exploited exposed API tokens to inject malicious code, harvesting credentials and exfiltrating data. These incidents underscore the need for stronger security practices in both development and dependency management. Dependency cooldowns are a critical defense. By delaying installs of recently published packages, developers give security teams time to detect and respond to threats. Tools like uv and pip v26.1 now support this strategy, but it’s not a silver bullet. Pair cooldowns with vulnerability scanning to ensure timely updates without compromising security. Maintainers must also secure their release workflows. Use trusted publishers, enforce 2FA, and lock dependencies to prevent unauthorized changes. These steps reduce the attack surface and protect users from compromised packages. The PyPI community is actively working on automated quarantining and improved reporting mechanisms to stay ahead of threats.

item.title: KV-botnet: Don't call it a comeback
item.description: On Lumen: KV-botnet is a stark reminder of how state-sponsored actors exploit critical infrastructure. The recent takedown effort by the FBI, supported by Lumen’s null-routing, disrupted a major botnet used for espionage. This shows the importance of proactive defense, especially in sectors where infrastructure is a key target. The botnet’s focus on SOHO routers and firewalls highlights a persistent threat. These devices, often overlooked, provide a foothold for attackers to build covert networks. The operators’ attempts to re-exploit devices after takedown efforts underscore the need for continuous monitoring and rapid response. Supply chain security must be a priority. Compromised edge devices can serve as entry points for larger attacks. Organizations should ensure their infrastructure is resilient, with updated patches and robust detection mechanisms. This is not just about reacting to threats—it’s about anticipating them. The collaboration between law enforcement and private sector defenders is crucial. It sets a precedent for how we can collectively counter sophisticated cyber threats. As we move toward more AI-driven security, we must integrate these lessons into our strategies for better protection.

item.title: Finding Gadgets Like it’s 2026
item.description: On Atredis Partners: Java deserialization vulnerabilities have long been a focal point for security research. Over the years, the Java ecosystem has made strides to reduce the risk, but the complexity of gadget chains remains a challenge. Traditional methods like ysoserial have become outdated, and the research process has grown increasingly manual and unapproachable. This is where LLMs can make a difference. By combining static analysis, reasoning, and implementation skills, they can automate the discovery of new gadget chains. In just two days, we implemented a new methodology that identified several novel chains, including one targeting WildFly and potentially other servers. The tooling leverages a call graph built with WALA and ASM to map out potential paths. An LLM agent queries this graph, builds test harnesses, and iteratively validates chains. This feedback loop helps eliminate false positives and refines the search. The result is a more efficient and effective approach to gadget discovery. One of the most interesting findings was a novel chain leveraging a shaded copy of the TemplatesImpl class in WildFly. This chain bypasses JPMS restrictions by using a shaded JAR, demonstrating how LLMs can uncover previously unknown attack vectors.

item.title: GitHub - luckyPipewrench/agent-egress-bench: Open Apache-2.0 corpus, runner, scoring, and result-verification contracts for measuring AI-agent egress controls. A PipeLab open project.
item.description: On GitHub: Agent Egress Bench offers a shared yardstick for evaluating how well tools control AI agent egress. It’s tool-agnostic and built to test the security layer, not the model itself. This aligns with my focus on governance and control in agentic systems. The framework ensures transparency by defining clear contracts for runners, scoring, and evidence. Every result is scoped to a specific product, version, and configuration. This makes comparisons meaningful over time. The repository includes a reference adapter for Pipelock, showing how the benchmark applies in practice. It’s a practical way to measure containment and false positives without vendor bias. The tool emphasizes reproducibility and offline verification. A reader can validate a result without relying on the original runner. This is critical for trust in security claims. The framework also separates how a run happened from what was found, ensuring clarity in reporting. For teams building or evaluating agentic AI systems, this is a valuable resource. It supports governance, audit, and control by providing a standardized way to measure and compare security tool performance. The open nature of the project invites collaboration and ensures the framework evolves with industry needs.

item.title: Abusing Modern Browser Features for Phishing
item.description: On Certitude Consulting: The article highlights how modern browser features can be abused for phishing. A malicious site can freeze the GPU, enter fullscreen mode, and display a fake login screen. This attack leverages WebGL and the Fullscreen API to hide the phishing attempt from the user. The result is a convincing Windows login screen that mimics legitimate behavior. The same-origin policy and iframe techniques allow attackers to embed Google One Tap dialogs. By manipulating CSS and positioning elements, they can replicate a real login screen. This makes the phishing attempt more credible and harder to detect. The attack relies on social engineering and technical exploitation to trick the user. Zero Trust principles are critical here. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) remains a strong defense against credential phishing. Even if an attacker captures a password, MFA adds a second layer of protection. Organizations should prioritize MFA and phishing-resistant technologies like smartcards or hardware tokens. Awareness and training also play a key role in reducing risk. This research underscores the need for robust security practices. Browsers should enforce stricter fullscreen and keyboard lock controls. Enterprises must implement Zero Trust frameworks, enforce MFA, and educate users on recognizing phishing attempts. The goal is to create a secure environment where even sophisticated attacks are less likely to succeed.

item.title: Malicious npm Package in Baileys Fork (Skyzopedia Case)
item.description: On Xygeni: The runtime code injection in the npm package @dappaoffc/baileys-mod highlights a new frontier in supply chain attacks. This malicious fork of Baileys silently subscribes a bot session to attacker-controlled channels through a delayed payload. The injection occurs at runtime, evading install-time detection. The attack leverages trusted GitHub as a control channel, dynamically updating its payload without new npm versions. It mimics legitimate behavior, making it indistinguishable from user-initiated actions. This underscores the need for runtime-aware analysis beyond traditional scanning. The malicious code uses an IIFE to execute after an 80-second delay, fetching a JSON list of newsletter IDs from a GitHub raw URL. It spaces requests to avoid rate-limit detection and suppresses errors, further hiding its presence within the core library. Supply chain security must evolve to detect such sophisticated attacks. Full-source inspection, dependency risk correlation, and runtime behavior analysis are critical. This case shows that trust in forks and updates can be exploited, requiring layered defenses beyond registry takedowns.

item.title: GitHub - gendigitalinc/sage: Lightweight Agent Detection & Response (ADR) layer for AI agents — guards commands, files, and web requests. Part of Gen Agent Trust Hub.
item.description: On GitHub: Sage offers a lightweight security layer for AI agents that intercepts and checks tool calls before execution. This approach aligns well with agentic AI governance by adding a proactive defense against dangerous actions. It's a practical tool for securing AI agents in environments where control and audit are critical. The multi-layered detection includes URL reputation, local heuristics, and prompt injection defenses. These features help mitigate risks like command injection and credential exposure. For teams focused on AI governance, this provides a solid foundation for securing agent behavior without compromising performance. Sage's integration with existing platforms and support for multiple threat detection methods make it a flexible solution. It's especially valuable for organizations that need to enforce strict compliance and control over AI agent activities. This kind of tool helps bridge the gap between innovation and security in agentic AI systems. For those looking to implement governance and control in agentic AI, Sage offers a real-world example of how to secure the stack. It's a useful addition to any security strategy focused on AI agents and their interactions with external systems.

item.title: Introducing Trusted Access for Cyber
item.description: On OpenAI: GPT‑5.3‑Codex represents a significant leap in cyber-capable models. Its ability to work autonomously for extended periods can enhance threat detection and remediation. However, this power introduces new risks that require careful management. OpenAI’s Trusted Access for Cyber aims to address these challenges by focusing on trust and identity. This approach aligns with my work on agentic AI orchestration and AI governance. The core of Trusted Access for Cyber is placing advanced capabilities in the right hands. This mirrors the need for trust-based frameworks in deploying frontier models for enterprise security. Just as we build Zero Trust architectures, we must ensure models are used responsibly. The balance between enabling innovation and preventing misuse is critical. OpenAI’s pilot program reflects a broader industry shift toward responsible deployment. By prioritizing defenders first, they’re addressing the ambiguity of intent in cyber actions. This is a step toward reducing friction for good-faith work while maintaining security. It’s a model that resonates with the principles of AI governance and risk management. The $10 million API credits for the Cybersecurity Grant Program further underscores the importance of accelerating defensive capabilities. It’s a practical step toward raising the baseline of security across the ecosystem. As we continue to explore agentic AI and multi-agent orchestration, these frameworks will become increasingly vital.

item.title: AI Playbook for Security Teams
item.description: On Island: The nine entry points in the AI playbook highlight where agents and AI systems enter the enterprise. These points are critical for understanding exposure and ensuring visibility. As security teams grapple with the rapid adoption of AI, it's clear that traditional tools like DLP and endpoint protection are no longer sufficient. The playbook provides a framework to identify gaps and align with the necessary controls. A unified control plane is essential for managing AI at scale. The playbook emphasizes that piecing together multiple point solutions is inefficient and leaves gaps. A single control plane can provide comprehensive coverage across all nine entry points, ensuring consistency and reducing complexity. This approach aligns with the need for governance, audit, and control in agentic AI environments. The AI maturity assessment and checklist offer a practical way to evaluate readiness. Before scaling AI, organizations must address 40 key controls. These include agent visibility, identity management, model choice, and app publishing. The playbook underscores the importance of governance and compliance in every stage of AI deployment. This is where my expertise in frameworks like NIST CSF and ISO 27001 becomes relevant. Security teams must lead the charge in integrating AI with existing security strategies. The playbook serves as a guide to transition from reactive to optimized AI adoption. It's about building a resilient infrastructure that supports innovation while maintaining control. This is the foundation of agentic AI governance and the path forward for secure, scalable AI.

item.title: CADR for dummies
item.description: On Oligo: Cloud application security is evolving fast—but the answer doesn’t have to be complicated. CADR focuses on runtime behavior instead of static configurations. This approach helps separate real threats from noise by looking at what’s actually happening in running applications. It’s a shift from traditional tools that miss the early signs of attacks. Runtime is where modern threats live. Attacks often start in code, dependencies, and APIs—not at the perimeter. CADR gives deep visibility into these areas, catching issues before they escalate. This is critical for protecting production environments and reducing the time to respond. CADR unifies protection across apps, cloud, network, and AI. Attacks move freely between layers, and CAD’s runtime-driven model tracks them effectively. By correlating signals from different sources, it creates a full picture of what’s happening in real time. This helps reduce blind spots and improves overall security. Securing AI and agentic systems is especially tricky. Static controls don’t cut it here. CADR’s approach addresses this by focusing on runtime behavior. It helps manage the unique risks of these environments, where traditional methods fall short. This is a game-changer for modern security strategies.

item.title: Shadow AI Trial
item.description: On Push Security: Shadow AI is becoming a critical security risk, especially with the rise of LLMs and agentic AI. These tools often operate in the browser, where they interact with sensitive data and external services. Traditional network and endpoint tools miss this activity, leaving organizations blind to what’s happening. The browser is the only place where you can see the full picture of AI usage across your environment. The visibility provided by tools like Push Security is essential. They capture live telemetry from browser sessions, identifying both sanctioned and shadow AI apps. This helps security teams understand what’s being used, how data is being handled, and where risks lie. It’s a practical way to govern AI usage without disrupting workflows. Push Security offers a flexible approach to managing shadow AI. It starts with Monitor mode, recording usage patterns without intervention. This builds a baseline for risk assessment. As policies mature, you can transition to Acknowledge or Block modes, ensuring users are guided or restricted appropriately. This progression makes governance scalable and manageable. Automated categorization and per-team controls are game changers. They reduce the manual effort needed to manage AI tool access, especially as new tools emerge. By aligning governance with team needs, you can balance innovation with security. This is how you stay ahead of shadow AI risks in a rapidly evolving landscape.

item.title: HEIF Heist
item.description: On Heif Heist: The HEIF Heist exposes a critical flaw in how image processing pipelines are handled across multiple platforms. By targeting native C/C++ decoders like libheif and libde265, attackers can bypass application-level protections and achieve RCE or data leaks. This isn't just a single vulnerability but a class of issues affecting a wide ecosystem. The implications for supply chain security are significant. Many systems rely on these decoders indirectly through wrappers or prebuilt images, making them a common attack surface. Isolating image processing and applying strict update policies can mitigate these risks, especially in regulated environments where compliance is paramount. This highlights the need for robust pipeline isolation and continuous patching. Even if RCE isn't immediately possible, the potential for data exposure remains high. Teams must treat image processing as a critical security layer, not an afterthought.

item.title: File Notification Attacks
item.description: On Inoti: File-notification systems are a critical but often overlooked attack surface. Across Linux, Android, Windows, and macOS, these systems leak user behavior through file events, even when files themselves are unreadable. On Linux, watching a readable directory reveals all file activity, including keystrokes. On Android, apps can bypass privacy protections to monitor private folders like WhatsApp’s media. Windows is particularly vulnerable, as watching the root directory exposes full file paths, including real-time website visits. These flaws highlight the need for stronger access controls and rethinking how we handle cross-user notifications in enterprise environments. The root issue is that file-notification systems expose metadata, not content. This allows attackers to infer timing, file existence, and even application behavior. For example, inter-keystroke timing leaks can reveal typing patterns, while file events track when media is sent or received. These attacks don’t require direct file access, making them hard to detect. Enterprise environments must audit their use of file-notification APIs and enforce strict permissions to prevent cross-user exploitation. Modern systems like Linux and Windows have partial mitigations, but many attacks still work out-of-the-box. For instance, Windows’ undocumented behavior remains a risk unless policies are explicitly enabled. This underscores the importance of regular security audits and staying informed about emerging threats. As we increasingly rely on file-notification systems for automation and monitoring, we must ensure they’re designed with security in mind from the start.

item.title: PhantomRaven: NPM Malware Hidden in Invisible Dependencies
item.description: On Web archive: PhantomRaven shows how supply chain attacks can bypass traditional tools. Attackers used invisible dependencies to hide malicious code from most security systems. These packages appeared clean but fetched harmful code at install time. This technique exploits a gap in how many tools analyze dependencies. The malware automatically runs during npm install, stealing credentials and system details. It targets CI/CD environments and builds profiles of compromised systems. Developers unknowingly install these packages, often based on AI suggestions that sound legitimate. This isn't just a theoretical risk. Thousands of developers are affected. Tools that only check package metadata miss the real threat. We need solutions that monitor actual behavior, not just what packages claim to do.

item.title: WeWorm
item.description: On Calif: WeWorm demonstrates how AI accelerates zero-click attacks in mobile ecosystems. By leveraging AI, we discovered and exploited a vulnerability in WeChat’s VoIP stack in just two days. This led to the creation of a worm that spreads through calls without user interaction. The speed and scale of this attack highlight the urgent need for AI governance and faster vulnerability remediation. The worm hijacks WeChat accounts by exploiting a memory corruption issue. Once compromised, the attacker can send messages, make calls, and spread to new victims. The exploit works even if the victim doesn’t answer the call, making detection nearly impossible. This underscores the fragility of trust in mobile ecosystems and the risks of unpatched vulnerabilities. AI enables both the discovery and execution of such attacks, but it also offers a path to faster mitigation. Traditional methods took months to build a worm of this scale. With AI, the same can be done in weeks. The key is to use these tools responsibly, ensuring they empower defenders rather than attackers. WeWorm is a wake-up call for AI security and governance. It shows how quickly vulnerabilities can be weaponized, especially in apps with broad reach like WeChat. The solution lies in collaboration between governments, industry, and researchers to secure the supply chain and accelerate patching. The future of security depends on it.

item.title: Anyone Can Buy Data Tracking US Soldiers and Spies to Nuclear Vaults and Brothels in Germany
item.description: On Wired: The unregulated sale of location data is exposing US military and intelligence operations to unprecedented risks. Commercial data brokers are providing foreign adversaries with detailed insights into the movements of service members and contractors stationed abroad. This data reveals daily routines, access patterns, and even personal habits, all of which could be weaponized for espionage or sabotage. The implications are severe, especially when it comes to sensitive installations like nuclear storage facilities or intelligence hubs. U The problem isn't just about privacy—it's about national security. Location data can expose critical infrastructure, guard schedules, and operational weaknesses. Adversaries could use this information to target personnel, compromise systems, or disrupt military readiness. The data is often collected through unregulated means, making it difficult to trace or control. Even the most basic movements—like a trip to a base cafeteria—can provide valuable intel to those with malicious intent. U The current legal and regulatory framework is inadequate to address this growing threat. While there are policies in place, they often lack the enforcement power needed to protect service members and their families. The solution requires stronger governance around data collection, clearer definitions of protected sites, and stricter oversight of data brokers. It also demands a cultural shift within the military and government to prioritize operational security in an era where digital footprints are as revealing as physical ones. U

item.description: On Anthropic: Project Glasswing highlights the accelerating pace of AI-driven cybersecurity threats. Models like Claude Mythos Preview can now find and exploit vulnerabilities that have evaded human experts for years. This underscores the need for proactive defense frameworks that integrate AI into security operations. The collaboration across industry giants and open-source communities in Project Glasswing is a critical step. By leveraging AI to identify and patch flaws, we can shift from reactive to predictive security. Governance and transparency must guide these efforts to prevent misuse and ensure responsible innovation. Securing critical infrastructure requires more than technology—it demands shared responsibility. As AI capabilities evolve, so must our strategies for risk mitigation and incident response. Project Glasswing sets a precedent for collective action, blending technical expertise with ethical oversight. The future of cybersecurity hinges on balancing innovation with accountability. We must build systems that harness AI’s power while safeguarding against its potential for harm. Collaboration, standards, and continuous improvement will define our success in this new era.

item.title: The Strava Heat Map Shows Even Militaries Can't Keep Secrets from Social Data
item.description: On Wired: Strava's heat map has exposed how operational security can be compromised by seemingly innocuous data shared online. The public visibility of fitness activity data from military and intelligence personnel has revealed patterns of life that could endanger individuals and facilities. This underscores the need for stricter data governance and privacy controls in sensitive environments. The incident highlights a broader challenge: the digital footprints left by personal devices and apps can expose secrets once thought secure. Whether it's tracking patrol routes or identifying individuals, the risks are real and growing. Organizations must adapt to this new reality by embedding privacy and security into their operations. Training and awareness are critical. Leaders and staff need to understand the implications of sharing data, especially in high-risk environments. Technology companies also have a role to play in designing features that prioritize security without compromising user experience. A proactive approach is essential to mitigate these risks.
